content: Professor Barbara Schneeman, an Emerita Professor from the Departments of Nutrition and Food Science and Technology at the University of California, Davis, United States, has contributed significantly to the field of nutrition policy and research. Professor Reema Tayyem, a Professor of Nutrition at the University of Jordan and Qatar University, has also been instrumental in advancing nutritional science in the Middle East. Dr. Alison Tedstone, who served as Chief Nutritionist at Public Health England from 2013 to 2022, has played a pivotal role in shaping public health nutrition policies in the United Kingdom. Associate Professor Anne Marie Thow, from the Menzies Centre for Health Policy and Economics at the University of Sydney, Australia, has focused on public policy and health economics. Professor Edelweiss Wentzel-Viljoen, an Extraordinary Professor of Nutrition at the Center of Excellence for Nutrition at North-West University, South Africa, has contributed to nutrition research in the African context. Dr. Angela Boland, from the Liverpool Reviews and Implementation Group at the University of Liverpool, United Kingdom, has led systematic reviews in public health. Professor Emma Boyland, a Professor of Food Marketing and Child Health in the Department of Psychology at the University of Liverpool, has conducted research on the impact of food marketing on children’s health. Dr. Andrew Jones and Dr. Lauren McGale, both from the Department of Psychology at the University of Liverpool, have contributed to behavioral studies related to food marketing. Professor Elie Akl, from the Department of Internal Medicine and the Department of Epidemiology and Population Health at the American University of Beirut, Lebanon, has served as a methods expert in evaluating public health interventions. Dr. Damian Francis, Co-Director of Cochrane Caribbean at the University of the West Indies, Jamaica, has also provided expertise in systematic reviews and evidence synthesis. Dr. Huda Mustafa Al Hourani, an Associate Professor in the Department of Clinical Nutrition and Dietetics at the Hashemite University, Jordan, has contributed to clinical nutrition research. Dr. Gershim Asiki, a Research Scientist at the African Population Health and Research Center in Kenya, has focused on population health. Dr. Suparna Ghosh-Jerath, a Professor and Head of Community Nutrition at the Indian Institute of Public Health, Delhi, has worked extensively on public health nutrition in India. Dr. Maria João Gregório, Director of the National Healthy Eating Promotion Program in Portugal, has led initiatives to improve dietary habits at the national level. Professor Boyd Swinburn, a Professor of Population Nutrition and Global Health at the University of Auckland, New Zealand, has been a leading figure in global health and nutrition policy. The WHO NUGAG Subgroup on Policy Actions has evaluated the impact of food marketing policies on children. The evidence suggests that mandatory policies, such as legally enforceable regulations, are more effective in reducing children’s exposure to food marketing compared to voluntary measures. Studies indicate that voluntary measures often show undesirable effects for public health, whereas mandatory policies are associated with more favorable outcomes. The subgroup also assessed the impact of food marketing policies on various outcomes, including dietary intake, food purchasing, and exposure to marketing. The evidence on the effectiveness of these policies remains uncertain due to inconsistencies and methodological limitations in the studies. For example, while some studies reported reductions in exposure to food marketing and unhealthy food purchasing, others showed no significant effects. Policies targeting children over 12 years of age were more likely to show favorable outcomes compared to those targeting younger children. Additionally, government-led nutrient profile models used to classify foods for marketing restrictions were more effective than company-specific models. The subgroup highlighted the need for further research to evaluate the long-term impact of food marketing policies on health outcomes, such as obesity, dietary-related non-communicable diseases (NCDs), and food preferences. The evidence on these outcomes is currently very limited or unavailable. The WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of implementing mandatory policies to protect children from the harmful effects of food marketing. These policies should be aligned with human rights standards, consider equity and acceptability, and address barriers to implementation and enforcement.
